title: Rethinking Hate Speech Detection on Social Media: Can LLMs Replace Traditional Models?
measurement_description: The paper evaluates the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) compared to traditional BERT-based models in detecting hate speech, specifically focusing on code-mixed and transliterated contexts. As part of this, it measures how well the models identify hate speech targeting various religious communities across different datasets, capturing both direct and implicit/subtle religious hate.
findings: The study found that expressions of religious hate vary significantly depending on the dataset: IndoHateMix captures code-mixed hate aimed at Hindus, Muslims, and Sikhs often intertwined with political hostility; HateXplain demonstrates explicit and direct hostility mainly targeting Muslims and Jews; and ImplicitHate features more subtle, hidden stereotypes directed at Muslims. In evaluating the models, LLMs (particularly LLaMA3.1-8B) significantly outperformed traditional transformer models like mBERT in identifying these varied, context-heavy, and code-mixed forms of religious and political hate speech.
